newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia watchdog urges investment fund listing.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia watchdog urges investment fund listing.

text.p: Slovenia's securities market watchdog on Monday called on investment funds involved in the privatisation process to list their shares on the over-the-counter (OTC) bourse as soon as possible.
"That is the only way to regulate current trading on the grey market," Igor Kusar, head of the Securities' Market Agency, told investors at an annual bourse conference.
But the Association of Slovenian Investment Funds said it would only list its shares after parliament passed a law that would offer additional state capital in exchange for privatisation vouchers.

"We will ask for a listing on the OTC market of the Ljubljana bourse as soon as a law which determines what capital will be offered for vouchers is passed," Andrej Urbas, president of the association, said.

Under Slovenia's privatisation scheme, which started in 1994 and involved some 1,500 companies, every citizen received a voucher whose value varied with their age, from 100,000 tolars ($645) for people under 18 to 400,000 for those over 48.
Holders could place the voucher directly into companies or into 72 investment funds which later exchanged them for stakes in companies that were privatised.

The funds have so far collected 320 billion tolars of privatisation vouchers, or 57 percent of all vouchers issued, but only managed to exchange a third of them for capital, due to a lack of capital available and partly due to the slow pace of privatisation.
Funds said the amount of vouchers issued exceeded the capital available by about 136 billion tolars.
In October 1996 the government said it would prepare a law granting additional capital in exchange for vouchers by January this year but it has not done so yet.

Funds said the additional capital could consist of government stakes in petrol firms Petrol and Istrabenz, telecommunication company Telekom, port Luka Koper, airport Aerodrom Ljubljana, gas firm Geoplin, electricity firms, banks and insurarers.
So far the government has not yet decided what companies it would offer.
Currently shares of the funds are being traded at about 10 percent of their nominal value on the grey market and analysts said the price was unlikely to rise before funds were listed on the bourse.
"When the funds are listed on the bourse, their price is likely to rise because the number of those buying their shares will probably increase," Kusar said.

"I expect the funds will be traded at a maximum of 20 to 30 percent of their nominal value after they are listed because of the low number of vouchers that have already been exchanged for stakes in companies," an analyst said. ($ = 155.0 Slovenian Tolar)
